'''tufter''' (tuf′tėr), ''n.'' [< ''tuft''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] A staghound employed to drive a deer out of cover. ''Encyc. Brit.'', XII. 394.

'''tuftgill''' (tuft′gil), ''n.'' A tuft-gilled fish, or lophobranch.

'''tuft-gilled''' (tuft′gild), ''a.'' Having tufted gills; cirribranchiate or lophobranchiate. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') Noting the tooth-shells or ''Dentaliidæ.'' See ''Cirribranchiata'', and cut under ''tooth-shell.'' (''b'') Noting the sea-horses and related fishes. See ''Lophobranchii'', and cuts under ''Hippocampidæ'', ''pipe-fish'', and ''Solenostomus.''}}

'''tuft-hunter''' (tuft′hun″tėr), ''n.'' One who seeks or covets the society of titled persons; one who courts the acquaintance of celebrities at any sacrifice of personal dignity; a toady; a sycophant. {{smaller|The term took its rise at the English universities from a tuft worn on the cap by young noblemen. [Slang, Eng.]}}
{{smaller block|At Eton a great deal of snobbishness was thrashed out of Lord Buckram, and he was birched with perfect impartiality. Even there, however, a select band of sucking ''tuft-hunters'' followed him. ''Thackeray'', Book of Snobs, v.

He was at no time the least of a ''tufthunter'', but rather had a marked natural indifference to tufts.
{{right|''Carlyle'', Sterling, ii. 3.}}}}

'''tuft-hunting''' (tuft′hun″ting), ''n.'' The practice of a tuft-hunter. ''Dickens'', Our Mutual Friend, i. 8.

'''tufting-button''' (tuf′ting-but″on), ''n.'' A style of button used in upholstery. See ''tuft''<sup>2</sup>, ''v. t.'', 3. ''Car-Builder’s Dict.''

'''tuft-moccado†''' (tuft′mok″a̤-dō), ''n.'' Tufted moccado. See ''moccado.''

Browne'', Britannia’s Pastorals, i. 5.}}}} '''tug''' (tug), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''tugged'', ppr. ''tugging''. [< ME. ''tuggen'', ''toggen'', ''togen'', a secondary form of ''tukken'', pull: see ''tuck''1, ''tow''1, ''tee''1.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To pull or draw with sturdy effort or violent strain; haul with force; pull. {{smaller block|''Togyd'' with tene [sorrow] was god of prys; To don hym sorwe was here delys [their delight]; He seyde no word loth. {{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Pearson, IV. 119).}}}} {{smaller block|As when a slaughter’d bull’s yet-reeking hide, Strain’d with full force, and ''tugg’d'' from side to side, The brawny curriers stretch. {{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xvii. 451.}}}} {{smaller block|And [the satyrs] ''tug'' their shaggy Beards, and bite with Grief the Ground. {{right|''Congreve'', Death of Queen Mary.}}}} '''2.''' To tow by means of a steam-tug: as, the vessel had to be ''tugged'' into port. '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To pull with great effort; haul; drag. {{smaller block|The meaner sort [of Dalmatians] will ''tug'' lustily at one oare. {{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 2.}}}} '''2.''' To exert one’s self; labor; strive; struggle; contend; wrestle. The seas are rough and wider Than his weak arms can ''tug'' with. {{smaller block|{{right|''Ford'', Perkin Warbeck, v. 2.}}}} They ''tug'', they strain!—down, down they go, The Gael above, Fitz-James below. {{smaller block|{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., v. 16.}}}} '''tug''' (tug), ''n.'' [< ''tug'', ''v.''; in part ult. a var. of ''tow''2, a rope, etc., and connected with ''tie''1, a band, rope, etc.; all from the ult. verb represented by ''tee''1.] '''1.''' The act of pulling, dragging, or hauling with effort, exertion, or difficulty. The idle vessel slides that wat’ry way, Without the blast or ''tug'' of wind or oar. {{smaller block|{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, iv. 3.}}}} '''2.''' A supreme effort; the severest strain or struggle; a contest; wrestle; tussle. {{smaller block|She had seen from the window Tartar in full ''tug'' with two carriers’ dogs, each of them a match for him in size. {{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Shirley, xx.}}}} '''3.''' A vehicle used in some parts of England for conveying timber or fagots. {{smaller block|I have seen one tree on a carriage which they call there [in Sussex] a ''Tug'', drawn by twenty-two oxen. {{right|''Defoe'', Tour through Great Britain, I. 204. (''Davies.'')}}}} '''4.''' A small but powerful steam-vessel, whether screw or paddle, constructed for the purpose of towing other vessels.—'''5.''' A chain, strong rope, or leather strap used as a trace; a trace (of a harness). {{smaller block|It [tugge] signifieth the pull or draught of the oxen or horses, and therefore the leathers that beare the chiefe stresse of the draught the cartars call then ''tugges.'' {{right|''Puttenham,'' Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 229.}}}} {{smaller block|My fur ahin’ [off wheel-horse] ’s a wordy [worthy] beast As e’er in ''tug'' or tow was trac’d. ''Burns,'' The Inventory.}} '''6.''' In ''mining,'' an iron hoop to which a tackle is affixed.—'''To hold one tug†''', to keep one busily employed; keep one in work. {{smaller block|There was work enough for a curious and critical Antiquary, that would ''hold him tugg'' for a whole yeare. {{right|''Life of A. Wood'' (by himself), p. 206.}}}} '''To hold tug†''', to stand severe handling or hard work.—'''Tug of war.''' (''a'') A severe and laborious contest. {{smaller block|When Greeks join’d Greeks, then was the ''tug of War.'' {{right|''Lee,'' Alexander the Great, iv. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|(''b'') An athletic contest in which a number of persons, generally four on each side and limited to a certain weight, tug at the ends of a rope, each side trying to pull the rope from the other, or to pull the other side over a line marked on the ground between the contestants. Also called ''rope-pull.''}} '''tugan,''' ''n.'' Same as ''tucan.'' '''tugboat''' (tug′bōt), ''n.'' A strongly built steamboat used for towing sailing and other vessels; a towboat; a tug. '''tug-carrier''' (tug′kar″i-ėr), ''n.'' An attachment to the back-strap of a wagon-harness. ''E. H. Knight.'' '''tugger''' (tug′ėr), ''n.'' One who tugs, or pulls with effort. {{smaller block|The ''tuggers'' at the oar. ''William Morris,'' Sigurd, i.}} '''tuggingly''' (tug′ing-li), ''adv.'' With laborious pulling.
